title: Core idioms: Or_error, labelled iteration and Map
body: Jane Street's `Base` and `Core` replace parts of the standard library with a consistent, labelled, monomorphic style. `open Core` shadows `List`, `String`, `Map` and others, so higher-order functions take their function as a labelled `~f` argument: `List.map xs ~f:square`. The labels let you pipe with `|>` and partially apply without caring about argument order.

Polymorphic comparison is deliberately hidden. `=` works on `int` only, and `String.equal`, `Int.compare` and friends are explicit. Containers take the comparison in as a first-class module: `Map.of_alist_reduce (module String) pairs ~f:( + )` states the key type once, which is the idiom that replaces functor application at the call site.

`Or_error.t` is `('a, Error.t) result`, where `Error.t` is a lazily built message that can carry s-expressions and context. Build errors with `Or_error.errorf`, combine a list with `Or_error.all`, and sequence steps with the `Or_error.Let_syntax` operators (`let%map`, `let%bind`). It is the default error type in Jane Street code because callers rarely need to match on the reason.
challenge: src/scores.ml has stubs. Implement `parse_entry` so "ada=3" gives `Ok ("ada", 3)` and malformed input gives an error, and `totals` so it sums values with the same key and returns the pairs sorted by name, stopping with the first parse error.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .`. The tests print results with `print_s [%sexp ...]`. Edit only src/scores.ml; the library already depends on core and ppx_jane.
question: How does `Map.of_alist_reduce (module String) pairs ~f` know how to compare keys?
correct: The first-class module argument supplies the comparison for the key type
wrong: It uses the polymorphic compare function
It converts every key to an int first
reasoning: Core containers take a first-class module carrying compare (and sexp) for the key type instead of relying on polymorphic comparison.
